fieldFixes.summary: Security firm Wiz found that Moltbook, a viral site where AI agents post and message each other, had left its production database open. The Supabase key in its client-side code was protected by no row-level security, so anyone could read and write 1.5 million API authentication tokens, 35,000 email addresses and private messages between agents, some containing plaintext OpenAI API keys. Wiz reported it on 31 January 2026 and it was fixed within hours. Another security researcher had found the same misconfiguration, which 404 Media reported. Wiz published its findings on 2 February 2026.

issues: All three quotes --check FOUND 2026-09-23 (noyb 23 June article; joint letter PDF; noyb open-letter page, which also has the 'constructive amendments have been tabled' sentence).

The summary calls the 18 June text 'the Council's position paper', which implies an adopted Council position. The European Parliament Legislative Train (Aug 2026 edition) says the Cypriot presidency prepared the Council negotiating mandate, and 'The vote in COREPER II to approve the Council negotiating mandate... which was scheduled for 26 June was ultimately cancelled'. Work continues under the Irish presidency. noyb itself calls the text 'the proposal for a final vote in the Council', and the coalition letter asks the Irish presidency to 're-insert Article 88b into their next compromise text'. So this was a presidency compromise text, not an adopted Council position. Title and summary corrected.

Summary says the letter insists 'dominant browser makers must not control' the signals. The annex actually says dominant companies 'should not be able to design or manage automated signals for users in a way that further entrenches their market power' and that dominant browsers and mobile operating systems 'should be required to facilitate' users sending signals. Reworded to match.

The letter is addressed to MEPs and the co-rapporteurs, the Permanent Representatives and Irish Ambassador O'Donoghue (Council presidency), and EVP Virkkunen and Commissioner McGrath. The 'MEPs, the Council and the Commission' wording is fine.

The significance says Article 88b decides whether software can 'carry the person's terms'. Article 88b concerns consent/refusal signals, not contractual terms (the letter: 'an obligation to respect automated signals that communicate users' privacy choices'). Adjusted to 'privacy choices'.
Source 1 and 2 dates: noyb dates the open-letter post 10.09.2026 (datePublished 2026-09-10). The letter PDF itself carries no date beyond its file name. Both source dates set to 2026-09-10.

Independent confirmation of the 18 June text: PPC Land (28 Jun 2026) reports the Council's 'latest position paper, published on 18 June 2026' removed Article 88b, and describes Article 88b in COM(2025) 837 as requiring controllers to accept and respect automated, machine-readable consent choices. Added it, together with the Legislative Train page.

fieldFixes.title: EU Council draft drops the machine-readable consent signal; 19 groups demand it back
fieldFixes.summary: According to noyb, the Council compromise text of 18 June 2026 on the Digital Omnibus removed Article 88b, the proposed obligation to respect automated, machine-readable signals of users' privacy choices. The text was the Cypriot presidency's draft Council negotiating mandate. The COREPER vote on that mandate, set for 26 June, was cancelled, and work passed to the Irish presidency. On 10 September 2026 a coalition of 19 civil-society organisations, businesses and academics ('Kill the cookie banner') wrote to MEPs, the Council presidency and member states' ambassadors, and the Commission asking for Article 88b to be restored. It insisted that 'independent user agents' must be able to transmit such signals, and that dominant companies such as browser gatekeepers must not be able to design or manage the signals in ways that entrench their market power. noyb reported that amendments to keep and strengthen Article 88b had been tabled in the European Parliament.
fieldFixes.significance: The fight over Article 88b is the live test of whether Europe will let a person's software, rather than each website's banner, carry the person's privacy choices.
